section.title: The Letter to the Exiles
section.sectionRationale: Jeremiah sends a letter to the first wave of exiles already carried off to Babylon, overturning the false hope of a quick return. Instead of resistance or despair, God calls His people to settle down, build, and seek the peace of the very city that holds them captive, while still promising that after seventy years He will bring them home with a future and a hope.
section.thesis: God's word to the exiles is to live faithfully within Babylon rather than resist it, trusting a specific covenant promise of restoration after seventy years rather than the comforting lies of false prophets, so that verse 11's plans to prosper you is first of all a promise to the exiled nation as a whole, not a private guarantee of an easy life for any individual who claims it.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: instructions to settle in Babylon and seek the welfare of the city; the specific promise of restoration after seventy years, a future and a hope; judgment on the false prophets remaining in Jerusalem; the fiery death decreed for Ahab and Zedekiah who prophesied lies in Babylon; and the rebuke of Shemaiah for opposing Jeremiah's true word.

units.label: Settle down and seek the city's welfare

verses.text: This is the text of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders among the exiles and to the priests, the prophets, and all the others Nebuchadnezzar had carried into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.
(This was after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the court officials, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metalsmiths had been exiled from Jerusalem.)
The letter was entrusted to Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to King Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon. It stated:
This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says to all the exiles who were carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon:
“Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce.
Take wives and have sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters. Multiply there; do not decrease.
Seek the {{shalom|prosperity}} of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.”
For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “Do not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among you, and do not listen to the dreams you elicit from them.
For they are falsely prophesying to you in My name; I have not sent them, declares the LORD.”

units.label: Seventy years, then a future and a hope
units.note: a specific promise to a specific exile

verses.text: For this is what the LORD says: “When Babylon's seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place.
For I know the {{machashabah|plans}} I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.
Then you will call upon Me and come and pray to Me, and I will listen to you.
You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.

I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will {{shubshevut|restore}} you from captivity and gather you from all the nations and places to which I have banished you, declares the LORD. I will restore you to the place from which I sent you into exile.”

units.label: Judgment on the prophets left in Jerusalem

verses.text: Because you may say, “The LORD has raised up for us prophets in Babylon,”
this is what the LORD says about the king who sits on David's throne and all the people who remain in this city, your brothers who did not go with you into exile,

this is what the LORD of Hosts says: 
“I will send against them sword and famine and plague, and I will make them like rotten figs, so bad they cannot be eaten.

I will pursue them with sword and famine and plague. I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, a curse, a desolation, and an object of scorn and reproach among all the nations to which I banish them.

I will do this because they have not listened to My words, declares the LORD, which I sent to them again and again through My servants the prophets. And neither have you exiles listened, declares the LORD.”

units.label: Ahab and Zedekiah's lying prophecy
units.note: a curse and a fiery death

verses.text: So hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles I have sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.

This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says about Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying to you lies in My name: “I will deliver them to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will kill them before your very eyes.
Because of them, all the exiles of Judah who are in Babylon will use this curse: ‘May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire!’

For they have committed an outrage in Israel by committing adultery with the wives of their neighbors and speaking lies in My name, which I did not command them to do. I am He who knows, and I am a witness, declares the LORD.”

units.label: Shemaiah's opposition and judgment
units.note: a lie the exiles were made to trust

verses.text: You are to tell Shemaiah the Nehelamite that

this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “In your own name you have sent out letters to all the people of Jerusalem, to the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, and to all the priests. You said to Zephaniah:

‘The LORD has appointed you priest in place of Jehoiada, to be the chief officer in the house of the LORD, responsible for any madman who acts like a prophet, you must put him in stocks and neck irons.
So now, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who poses as a prophet among you?
For he has sent to us in Babylon, claiming: Since the exile will be lengthy, build houses and settle down; plant gardens and eat their produce.’”
(Zephaniah the priest, however, had read this letter to Jeremiah the prophet.)
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
“Send a message telling all the exiles what the LORD says concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite. Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you, though I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie,

this is what the LORD says: ‘I will surely punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. He will have no one left among this people, nor will he see the good that I will bring to My people, declares the LORD, for he has preached rebellion against the LORD.’”

shalom.gloss: Peace, welfare, wholeness, prosperity. Jeremiah tells the exiles to seek the shalom of Babylon itself and to pray for it, tying their own welfare to the welfare of the pagan city that holds them captive.

machashabah.gloss: A plan, thought, or purpose. God's machashabah for the exiles is fixed to the seventy-year timeframe just named in verse 10, a specific national promise of return, not a blank check for any individual reader's circumstances.

shubshevut.gloss: To restore from captivity, literally to turn or return a captivity. This recurring phrase across Jeremiah's later chapters, 30:3, 32:44, 33:7, names the specific covenant reversal God promises His exiled people.

basic.context: Jeremiah writes a letter from Jerusalem to the exiles already taken to Babylon in the first deportation. Rather than promising a quick return, as popular prophets were doing, he tells them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the good of the city that holds them, because God's actual plan is restoration only after seventy years.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real pastoral letter to a specific community in a specific crisis. Verse 11, plans to prosper you, is often quoted as a private promise, but in context it is God's plan for the whole exiled nation, tied to the seventy years of verse 10, not a guarantee of ease for any individual believer who claims it today.
basic.originalLanguages: God tells the exiles to seek the shalom, the welfare or peace, of Babylon itself. His machashabah, His plan, for them is a future and a hope, but it unfolds only after the shuv shevut, the reversal of their captivity, which He has already set at seventy years.
basic.typology: The exiles living as faithful sojourners in a pagan city, praying for its good while awaiting a promised homecoming, anticipates the New Testament picture of Christians as exiles and sojourners in the world, 1 Peter 2:11-12, seeking the good of the city while awaiting their true homeland.
basic.christ: The future and a hope promised here to national Israel finds its deepest fulfillment in Christ, in whom all of God's promises are yes and amen, 2 Corinthians 1:20. The pattern of God's good purposes for His exiled people, purposes for welfare and not for harm, is most fully secured for believers in the finished work of Jesus.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over the length of the exile, He names it at seventy years, and faithful to His covenant even while His people suffer its just consequences. He also confronts comforting lies spoken in His name with the same seriousness as any other sin, promising to hold false prophets accountable.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 9:2 shows Daniel reading this very promise of seventy years and being moved to prayer. 1 Peter 2:11-12 calls Christians to the same posture as exiles seeking the good of a foreign city. Romans 8:28 echoes God's purpose for good even within hardship. Matthew 24:24 warns of false prophets exactly like those Jeremiah confronts here.
basic.oneStory: God's word to His exiled people is not escape from Babylon but faithfulness within it, grounded in a specific promise of restoration and a future hope. That pattern, real hardship held together with a certain hope in God's good purposes, culminates in Christ, in whom every promise of future and hope is secured for God's people.

context.literary:
Chapter 29 is unusual in Jeremiah: it is a letter, and the book quotes it whole, with its covering note, its messengers and the controversy it started. The shape is a frame around a core. Verses 1 to 3 give the occasion and the couriers. The letter proper runs from verse 4 to verse 23, and it moves in four steps: the instruction to settle, verses 4 to 7; the warning about the prophets among them, verses 8 to 9; the promise of restoration, verses 10 to 14; and the sentence on those who stayed behind and on the false prophets of Babylon, verses 15 to 23. Verses 24 to 32 are the aftermath, a second letter, from Shemaiah, to the temple authorities in Jerusalem, and God's reply.

Notice how the promise is placed. The famous words of verse 11 sit inside a speech that begins with 'build houses' and ends with 'roasted in the fire.' The letter will not let comfort stand alone. The same speaker who promises a future and a hope also says that the people who stayed in Jerusalem will be like rotten figs, verses 17 to 19, and that the exiles too 'have not listened,' verse 19. The hope is real, and so is the verdict.

The chapter also works by a deliberate chain of names. Elasah and Gemariah carry the letter, verse 3. Ahab and Zedekiah are condemned, verse 21, and Shemaiah and Zephaniah appear in the sequel. Each name belongs to a family or office the reader knows from other chapters. Finally, the letter has a mirror in Jeremiah 24, the two baskets of figs, where the exiles are called the good figs. Chapter 29 shows what it means to be the good figs: not to sit and wait, but to build, plant, marry and pray.
context.historical:
The letter dates from about 594 or 593 BC, a few years after the first deportation of 597. The deportation of 2 Kings 24:14 had taken ten thousand of Jerusalem's leading people, the craftsmen and metalsmiths whom verse 2 names, and the exiles had been settled in Babylonia in communities, one of which Ezekiel names as by the Kebar canal, Ezekiel 3:15. Ezekiel himself was among them, Ezekiel 1:1 to 3, and Daniel's circle had been taken earlier, Daniel 1:1 to 6. These were people who had lost everything, who had been told by temple, throne and prophet that Jerusalem would never fall, and who had no instructions for living in a pagan city.

The prophets who filled that gap spoke of a swift return, which is what Hananiah had said in Jerusalem, Jeremiah 28:3. The exiles had their own prophets in Babylon, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, verse 21, who made the same promise. Their hope was politically dangerous. A community that expected to leave soon would not build, would not marry and would not pray for the place. Hearing that kind of hope, Nebuchadnezzar's officials could be expected to treat it as unrest, and the burning of the two prophets, verse 22, fits that setting.

The letter travelled with royal envoys, Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah sent to Babylon, verse 3. The Shaphan family were scribes and officials who had protected Jeremiah before, 26:24. Back in Jerusalem the letter provoked a counterattack. Shemaiah wrote to Zephaniah the priest, who held the office that Pashhur had held when he put Jeremiah in the stocks, Jeremiah 20:1 to 2. Zephaniah, however, read the letter to Jeremiah, verse 29, which shows how the temple establishment was divided.
context.canonical:
The letter is the hinge between Israel's old story and its new one. Its instruction to settle echoes the promise to Abraham that his family would multiply, Genesis 12:2, and the command 'Multiply there; do not decrease' repeats the creation blessing, Genesis 1:28, now spoken to a people outside the land. It takes the first steps toward a life of dispersion that the Jewish people would live for centuries, and it is the pattern for Daniel, Esther and Nehemiah, who prospered in foreign courts.

The promise of verses 12 to 14 is a deliberate echo of Deuteronomy. 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart' recalls Deuteronomy 4:29, and the promise to restore from captivity and gather from all the nations is that of Deuteronomy 30:3. The letter thus shows that exile is the very scenario the Torah foresaw and prepared for.

The seventy years join Jeremiah 25:11 to 12, 2 Chronicles 36:21, Daniel 9:2 and Zechariah 1:12. Daniel reads this letter's promise and prays, and Cyrus's decree, Ezra 1:1, is the fulfilment as the Chronicler sees it. The picture of seeking the welfare of the city has its New Testament counterpart in Paul's call to pray for kings and all in authority, 1 Timothy 2:1 to 2, and in Peter's call to live honourably among the Gentiles as foreigners and exiles, 1 Peter 2:11 to 12. The warning against false prophets is picked up in Jesus' words in Matthew 24:24, and the reference to 'a future and a hope' returns in the book's own next chapter: 'there is hope for your future,' 31:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah wanted the exiles to hear two things at once that they were reluctant to hear together: you will be there a long time, and God is not finished with you. He was fighting for the soul of a community. The prophets who promised a quick return were not only wrong about the calendar, they were teaching people to treat their present life as unreal, a waiting room to be endured. Jeremiah's counsel makes life in Babylon real. Houses, gardens, marriages and children are not distractions from God's promise but the form in which it will be kept, 29:5 to 6.

He also wanted them to understand that their welfare is bound up with the welfare of their captors: 'if it prospers, you too will prosper,' verse 7. That is an astonishing instruction to a conquered people. The letter makes prayer for the enemy's city an act of faithfulness. And it gives the hope its proper object. The exiles are to wait for the LORD to 'attend to' them, verse 10, not to scheme for their own deliverance. Hearing this, the first readers were to lay down both despair and false optimism.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The letter is a word to a particular group at a particular time, and it prescribes for them with precision: build, plant, marry, pray, wait for seventy years. It is not a general promise to every believer that God will arrange a comfortable life. Verse 11 stands in the middle of a letter that also announces plague on those who stayed behind, and the plans it speaks of are God's plans for a people, to be realised over seventy years, with most of its first hearers dead before the return.

The passage still carries real application, but by analogy and with care. Believers who live as foreigners in a world not yet redeemed, 1 Peter 2:11, can take from it the call to put down roots, to work for the good of the place they live in, and to pray for it, while holding their final hope in God's promise of restoration. They may take verse 11 as a revelation of God's character, that He thinks thoughts of peace toward His people, as long as they do not use it to deny that a faithful life can still include suffering, as the following verses of this very chapter show. Reading the verse as a private promise of success misses both its first audience and its larger meaning.

debates.question: How should Jeremiah 29:11 be used today?

views.label: Only as a promise to Israel in exile
views.case: The 'you' is plural, the context is seventy years, and the verse is addressed to the exiles of 597. Applying it to individuals ignores that the first readers who heard it would mostly die in Babylon. On this view the verse is a fact about God's covenant with Israel and should be quoted only in that setting.

views.label: As a window onto God's character toward His people
views.case: The verse reveals the settled disposition of God toward those He has chosen: plans for peace, not harm, a future and a hope. The New Testament says that all God's promises are yes in Christ, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and that He works for the good of those who love Him, Romans 8:28. Believers may therefore draw from it as long as they keep its setting.

views.label: As a personal promise of prosperity
views.case: Some use it to promise individual success. Defenders note that the verse says 'prosper,' using the word shalom, which is wellbeing in the widest sense, and that God does care for individuals. Critics respond that the text speaks to a community and promises restoration, not an easy road.

debates.bearing: The best readings keep the corporate setting, take the character of God from it, and hold both together with the suffering the letter assumes.

debates.question: How are the 'seventy years' to be counted?

views.label: A literal period of seventy years
views.case: One count runs from the first deportation in 605 to Cyrus's decree in 539 or 538, a period of about sixty-six to sixty-seven years. A second runs from the temple's destruction in 586 to its rebuilding in 516, a period of exactly seventy. Daniel 9:2 and 2 Chronicles 36:21 present the period as a fulfilled length, and Zechariah 1:12 uses it of Jerusalem's desolation.

views.label: A round number for a full lifetime
views.case: Seventy is a standard expression for the span of a life, Psalm 90:10, and also the number of a full and complete period. On this view the point is that God has fixed the length and that it is long enough that many will die in exile, 29:28.

views.label: A prophecy that Daniel reapplies
views.case: Daniel 9:24 reinterprets the seventy years as seventy 'sevens,' which shows that later Scripture treats the number as open to deeper fulfilment. The first fulfilment was the return under Cyrus, and the larger one is the finished work of Christ.

debates.bearing: All three agree on the point that matters for the letter: God sets the limit, and the exiles are to live well until it ends.

study.originalLanguages:
The letter's words are chosen with care. In verse 7 the promise 'if it prospers, you too will prosper' is a pun: in her shalom there will be shalom for you. The same noun is repeated and the exile's wellbeing is bound by sound as well as by sense to the city's.

The verb in verse 10, 'attend to you,' is paqad, which means to visit, to take notice and to appoint. It is the word of Jeremiah 27:22, where the vessels stay in Babylon 'until the day I attend to them again.' The same verb is used of God's visitations in judgment and in rescue alike, and so the phrase in verse 10 means that the God who had visited the nation in punishment will visit it in mercy. The next phrase, 'confirm My promise,' is literally 'establish My good word,' with the verb that means to make something stand. God's good word has been spoken already, and what remains is that He should make it stand.

Verse 11 closes with a pair of nouns: 'a future and a hope.' The first, acharit, means what comes after, the end or latter part of something, and the second, tiqvah, is a hope that waits with expectancy. The same two words are paired in 31:17, 'there is hope for your future,' and in Proverbs 23:18. The pairing tells the exiles that there is an 'after' and that it is not empty.

The call in verses 12 to 13 uses the verb darash for 'seek,' and Deuteronomy 4:29 has the same promise, 'you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart.' The exiles are being led to the very repentance that the Torah's exile texts expected.

In verse 8 the exiles are told not to listen to 'the dreams you elicit.' The Hebrew verb is a causative form of the root for dreaming, and translations differ over whether the prophets induce dreams or the people ask for them. Either way, the people share responsibility for the message they get.

Verse 23 calls the false prophets' conduct an 'outrage,' nevalah, a word used for grave breaches of Israel's covenant decency, as in Genesis 34:7 and Joshua 7:15. Their offence is not only a false oracle but a moral rot.

In verse 22 the verb 'roasted' is the one used of grain parched in fire, Leviticus 2:14, and in verse 26 the 'madman' is a word used of ecstatic or unbalanced behaviour, as in 2 Kings 9:11. The 'stocks' in the same verse are the very instrument with which Pashhur had punished Jeremiah, Jeremiah 20:2.

Verse 28's 'the exile will be lengthy' uses an adjective meaning long, and it is Shemaiah's own report of the letter, which shows that he understood its message and objected to it.

typology.type: The exiles as the good figs who build and pray
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah 24 called the exiles good figs, and Jeremiah 29 shows what the good figs do: settle, work and pray in a foreign city. Peter writes to believers as 'foreigners and exiles' and tells them to live honourably among the nations, 1 Peter 2:11 to 12, and Paul roots the same pattern in Philippians 3:20, where citizenship is in heaven. The escalation is that the home we await is the new Jerusalem, Hebrews 11:13 to 16, a better country. The type falls short since Israel's exile ended in a return to an earthly land, while the Christian's is not over until the new creation.

The limited exile, ending when God 'attends to' His people, anticipates the redemption of Christ at the right time, Galatians 4:4. Daniel's reading of the seventy years leads him to prayer and to Gabriel's revelation of the seventy sevens, Daniel 9:2 and 9:24 to 27, which sets the return from Babylon inside a larger movement toward the Messiah. The type's escalation is that the true release is from the bondage of sin, John 8:36. It falls short because the return from Babylon was partial, and the people were still under foreign rule when Jesus was born.

typology.type: Prayer for the city that holds you
typology.fulfillment: The exiles are asked to pray to the LORD for Babylon, the enemy city, 29:7. Jesus extends the pattern to enemies and persecutors, Matthew 5:44, and Paul asks that prayers be made for kings and all in authority, 1 Timothy 2:1 to 2. On the cross Jesus prays for those who crucify Him, Luke 23:34, which makes the exile's prayer for the hostile city the shadow of the greatest prayer. The type falls short in that Jeremiah's counsel aims at the city's peace for a time, while Christ's prayer aims at the forgiveness of its people.

study.christ:
This letter leads to Christ first by the figure of the people in exile who are called to a hope that depends on God's visiting them. Verse 10, 'I will attend to you,' uses the language that Zechariah takes up in the Benedictus: 'the God of Israel has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68. The visitation that Jeremiah promised at the end of seventy years finds its deepest meaning when the Dayspring from on high visits those who sit in darkness, Luke 1:78 to 79. When Jesus weeps over Jerusalem because it did not recognise 'the time of your visitation,' Luke 19:44, He uses the same idea in judgment.

It leads to Christ by the promise of seeking and finding. 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart,' verses 13 to 14, is what Jesus says to His own people, 'Seek and you will find,' Matthew 7:7. The Lord who promised to be found is the one who came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the hope. The 'future and a hope' of verse 11 comes in the New Testament as 'Christ in you, the hope of glory,' Colossians 1:27, and as the hope that is an anchor for the soul, Hebrews 6:19. The promise that God would gather His exiles from every nation, 29:14, is met in Jesus' gathering of the scattered children of God into one, John 11:52. And the peace that Jeremiah urged the exiles to seek for the city is given in its fullness by the one who is our peace, Ephesians 2:14.

The letter also gives a pattern for Christ's people: His disciples, whom He sends into the world, John 17:15 to 18, are told, like the exiles, to remain in it and to be good for it, to love their enemies and to pray for those who persecute them.

A caution is needed. Verse 11 is not itself a hidden promise of Jesus, and its first meaning is the restoration of the exiles. The link to Christ rests on the way the New Testament takes up the language of visitation, seeking and hope, and on the larger story in which the return from Babylon is a first, partial step.
study.god:
The letter's most striking claim about God is that He is the one who has 'sent' the exiles to Babylon, 29:4 and 29:7, and that the place of their punishment is also the place where He is to be served. The same God who scattered them is the one who commands them to build, to plant and to pray. The exile is not a place beyond His reach. It is a place in which He is fully present and active, and His word follows them there in the form of a letter.

He is a God who plans. 'I know the plans I have for you,' verse 11, does not describe a vague good will but a settled purpose with a date on it, seventy years. His foreknowledge here is not a distant fact but a comfort: the length of the exile is known and chosen, and so cannot be extended by Babylon's power or shortened by a false prophet's promise.

He is also a God of truth who deals sharply with deceit. The prophets who speak lies in His name are condemned because, as verse 23 says, 'I am He who knows, and I am a witness.' He sees the hidden conduct of the men who claim to speak for Him. And His justice is even-handed. The remnant in Jerusalem is condemned for not listening, verses 17 to 19, but so are the exiles, and the verse 19 addition 'neither have you exiles listened' prevents the good figs from boasting.

He is a God who is found. 'I will be found by you,' verse 14, is a promise as well as a statement: He hears prayer, verse 12, and responds to wholehearted seeking. The One who sent them into exile will gather them again, and He will do it as the God who keeps His promises in the face of history.

For worship, the letter teaches us to trust God in places we did not choose, to pray in them and to do honest work there. It teaches us that the hope of God's people is not escape but restoration, and that they can wait for it with patient joy.

crossReferences.note: The vision of the two baskets of figs, where God calls the exiles good figs and promises to build them up and plant them. Chapter 29 describes the life of the good figs, and 29:17 describes the bad figs left behind. The two chapters interpret each other.

The first announcement of the seventy years, with its judgment on Babylon at the end of the period. Chapter 29 repeats the number to people who needed to hear it, and shows that the length of their exile is God's decision and not Babylon's.

If Israel seeks the LORD from the lands of exile with all the heart, they will find Him. Jeremiah 29:13 repeats it almost word for word, showing that the exile letter is shaped by the Torah's own provision for exile.

Daniel reads the seventy years in the books and turns to prayer and confession. It is the best example of how a faithful exile used this promise: not for passive waiting but for repentance, and so it shows what 29:12 looks like in life.

The Chronicler closes his history with the seventy years completed and Cyrus's decree. He reads the exile as a Sabbath rest for the land and sees the promise of Jeremiah 29:10 kept, which makes it the end of the story of the old exile.

Ezekiel sits among the exiles at Tel Abib by the Kebar canal, a prophet to the same community. His book gives the other side of Jeremiah's letter: God's glory leaves the temple and comes to the exiles in Babylon.

'There is hope for your future' uses the same pair of words as 29:11, a future and a hope. The Book of Consolation gives the content of the hope that the letter only announces, and the two chapters stand as one promise.

Peter calls his readers foreigners and exiles and tells them to live honourably among the Gentiles. The letter to Babylon is the Old Testament model for a people who belong to another country while doing good in this one.

Paul asks for prayers for everyone, for kings and all in authority, so that believers may lead quiet lives. It is the New Testament counterpart to praying for the city's welfare in Jeremiah 29:7, applied to the church's life under pagan rulers.

All God's promises find their yes in Christ. It shows how the future and the hope of Jeremiah 29:11 can be received by believers today: not by detaching the verse from its setting but by seeing its fulfilment in the one in whom God's word is confirmed.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is the story of a people who lose their home and are brought home. Adam and Eve are driven from the garden, Genesis 3:23 to 24, and Cain settles east of Eden, Genesis 4:16. Abraham leaves his country and lives as a foreigner in the land of promise, Hebrews 11:9. Israel is a sojourner in Egypt and then in the wilderness. In every case God is the one who sends and the one who brings back. Jeremiah 29 is the moment at which exile becomes the settled condition of the people of God, and it gives them a way to live in it.

The letter answers a question that the book of Genesis had already raised: how can a people live under a blessing in a place of curse? The answer is the pattern of Joseph, Daniel and Esther: to build, to serve, to pray, and to wait for God. It is what Abraham's descendants were meant to be, a blessing in the midst of the nations, Genesis 12:3, and in seeking Babylon's welfare the exiles discover that they can be that even in captivity.

It also sets up the next stage. The seventy years end with Cyrus, and a remnant returns, but the old promises have not been fully kept, and the prophets of the return, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, still look ahead. The true restoration waits for the one who gathers the exiles from the ends of the earth, Mark 13:27, and who ends the exile of sin and death. Paul says that those who are in Christ were once 'foreigners to the covenants of promise,' but are now fellow citizens with God's people, Ephesians 2:12 and 2:19.

Until that day, the church lives in the letter's time. It is in Babylon, praying for it, working in it and refusing its idols, while waiting for the city whose architect and builder is God, Hebrews 11:10. In the new creation the exile ends for good: 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, and the nations walk by its light, Revelation 21:24. The people who were told to seek the welfare of a foreign city will inherit a city in which there is no more curse, Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah's letter instruct the exiles to do in Babylon?

options.text: Build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the welfare of the city that holds them captive.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7 give these specific, ordinary instructions for settled life in exile.

options.text: Prepare for an armed uprising against Babylon.
options.note: The letter's message is the opposite, settle in and seek the city's peace, not rebellion.

options.text: Refuse to marry or have children until the return to Jerusalem.
options.note: The letter explicitly commands the opposite, take wives, have children, multiply there.

options.text: Wait passively without engaging in the life of the city at all.
options.note: The command goes further than waiting, it calls for active building, planting, and prayer for the city.

quiz.q: According to verses 10 to 11, when will God restore the exiles, and for what purpose?

options.text: After Babylon's seventy years are complete, according to His plans to give them a future and a hope.
options.note: Verse 10 sets the specific timeframe and verse 11 names God's purpose in restoring them.

options.text: Immediately, within the same year the letter was written.
options.note: The text explicitly sets a seventy-year timeframe, not an immediate return.

options.text: Only once every exile has personally repented in perfect detail.
options.note: The promise is tied to the seventy years, not an individualized repentance quota.

options.text: At an unspecified, open-ended future time with no set length.
options.note: The passage is unusually specific, naming seventy years, not leaving the timeframe open.

quiz.q: How should Jeremiah 29:11's plans to prosper you best be understood in context?

options.text: As God's promise to the whole exiled nation of a specific future restoration after seventy years, not a private guarantee of an easy life.
options.note: The you is plural and the promise is explicitly bound to the seventy years just named.

options.text: As an unconditional promise that any individual believer will avoid all hardship.
options.note: This reads the corporate, exile-specific promise as a private guarantee it was never meant to be.

options.text: As a promise only about financial wealth for the exiles.
options.note: The promise concerns national restoration and hope, not primarily financial gain.

options.text: As a vague sentiment with no real content or timeframe.
options.note: The promise is specific and dated, tied to the seventy years, not vague at all.

quiz.q: What judgment does God pronounce on Ahab and Zedekiah in verses 21 to 23?

options.text: They will be delivered to Nebuchadnezzar and killed, becoming a byword for a curse because they prophesied lies and committed adultery.
options.note: Verses 21 to 23 specify both their crimes and their fiery death before the exiles' eyes.

options.text: They will be honored as true prophets for their comforting message.
options.note: The opposite occurs, they are condemned and executed for false prophecy.

options.text: They will simply be exiled a second time to a different land.
options.note: Their judgment is death, not a second exile.

options.text: Nothing happens to them; the text leaves their fate unresolved.
options.note: Verses 21 to 22 explicitly describe their execution and the curse named after them.

quiz.q: What does the seventy-year promise of exile and restoration anticipate in the rest of Scripture?

options.text: Daniel reading this very promise and being moved to fervent prayer for his people's restoration, Daniel 9:2.
options.note: Daniel explicitly cites Jeremiah's seventy years as the basis for his prayer of repentance and hope.

options.text: No later biblical figure ever refers back to this promise.
options.note: Daniel 9:2 directly references this exact promise from Jeremiah.

options.text: A promise that is quietly dropped and never fulfilled anywhere in Scripture.
options.note: The exile's end is treated in Scripture as a real, historical fulfillment of this timeframe.

options.text: A promise fulfilled only in a symbolic, non-literal sense with no historical referent.
options.note: Scripture treats the seventy years and the return from exile as a real historical event, not merely symbolic.

questions: Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of the very city that held them captive. What would it look like for you to seek the good of a place or circumstance you did not choose and do not want to be in?
The exiles were tempted to trust popular, comforting prophets over God's actual, harder word. Where are you tempted to prefer a comfortable message over what God has actually said?

Jeremiah 29:11 is often quoted alone, out of its exile context. How does reading it as a promise to a whole community, tied to a specific waiting period, change how you hold your own hopes for the future?
God's restoration came only after seventy years of waiting, not immediately. Where is God calling you to faithful patience rather than an immediate escape from hard circumstances?
Shemaiah tried to silence Jeremiah's true word because it was unwelcome. Have you ever tried to silence or avoid a true but unwelcome word from God?

translationNotes.note: The same Hebrew word shalom translates prosperity, prospers, and prosper across this verse, the well-being of the exiles is deliberately tied to the well-being of the pagan city holding them.

Babylon's seventy years is widely reckoned from the first deportation in 605 BC to the decree of Cyrus permitting return around 538 BC, a datable, historical fulfillment rather than a symbolic round number alone.
The plural you throughout this letter addresses the whole community of exiles; the singular application often given to this verse today is a later, careful extension, not its first meaning.
